Approval without a custodian

Every business already has an approval process: a policy, a request, a sign-off, a payment. This is that, with one difference — the part that holds the money cannot act on it.

Four things, and that is all

Strip away the technology and there are four:

ThingIn your languageThe one property that matters
A ruleA policy. "We pay this, to whoever meets these conditions."Published in advance, and fixed. It has a fingerprint, so "the policy we agreed" is a specific thing, not a shared memory.
A requestA claim, an invoice, an order.Anyone may raise one. Raising it confers no power whatsoever.
An approvalA signature on the sign-off sheet.Given only when the request matches the rule exactly. One approval, not a decision.
SettlementThe payment actually leaving.Happens only when enough approvals are in. Nobody performs it; it follows.

The four do not have to be four people. Whoever writes a rule need not be the one requesting against it, and neither need be the one approving. A rule is a public document: you can write your own, or approve against one somebody else wrote, having read it.

What is genuinely different

In a normal arrangement, something in the middle — a bank, a platform, a payments provider, your own server — holds the ability to move the money, and you rely on it behaving. Controls are things that thing agrees to apply to itself.

Here, the part in the middle holds the request but cannot act on it. Not "is configured not to" — cannot. Approval lives on separate devices, and the ledger will not settle anything without them.

The row that sells it

Most organisations do not have a problem making a payment. They have a problem controlling who may authorise which payment — and proving afterwards that the control held. "Approve only what matches this published rule, under this hourly limit, and only when two of these three devices agree" is an authorisation matrix that sits outside every system involved.

What you can decide

DecisionWhat it buys you
How many approversOne device for something routine; two of three where the loss would hurt. Raising it is a key change, not a rebuild.
Who holds themDifferent people, different places, different kinds of device. Collusion becomes the only route, and collusion is a different risk from a breach.
An hourly ceilingThe most an approver will approve per hour, whatever the rule permits. Your backstop for a rule that turns out to be wrong.
What is visibleApprovers can publish that they are on duty. Then "is our approval process actually running" is a page you look at, not a question you ask someone.

What it costs you in practice

  • Availability is the real risk, not theft. Requiring two of three is safer than one — until two devices are lost, and then nothing can be approved at all. Choose the number from how many independent losses you should survive, not from how nervous you feel.
  • A rule is only as good as its review. The system guarantees that what gets approved matches the rule. It cannot tell you the rule was a sensible one. That reading is the work, and it happens once, in advance, in the quiet.
  • Rehearse it. Stop the approvers that can act alone and confirm the rest behave as you expect. Organisations that skip this discover the arrangement does not work at the worst possible moment.
Said plainly

This removes the need to trust the machinery in the middle. It does not remove the need to decide what you are willing to pay for, to whom, and on whose approval. It makes those decisions explicit, reviewable and enforced — which is more than most arrangements manage, and less than magic.

The mechanics — every check an approver runs, and how to operate one — are in how it works. What is running right now is on the signers dashboard.
